Ashok Kumar Cnr No.: Dlse01-003265-2020 1. Sh. Sariq Ahmad S/o Sh. Abdul Ahmad R/o H.No. 23, Gali no.5, Rashid Market Extn., Krishna Nagar, Delhi. .....Petitioner Versus 1. Sh. Ashok Kumar Gandhi R/o H.No. H-5, Ground Floor, Lajpat Nagar-III New Delhi. ............Driver-cum-owner/Respondent no.1 2. Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Company 93, Ashoka Bhawan, Nehru Place, Delhi. ............Insurance company/Respondent no.2 Date of accident : 30.09.2019 Result of accident : Injury(Permanent disability) Date of filing of Dar : 28.09.2020 Date of Decision : 23.04.2025 Mact No.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 1 Of 21 Bk Award 1.
texts.facts: The present claim arises out of a detailed accident report (DAR), filed by the police in terms of the provision of Motor Vehicle Act in which claimant Sariq Ahmad (aged about 41 years) sustained injuries. 2. Brief facts of the case are that on 30.09.2019, claimant was returning from Niti Bagh to his house on his motorcycle bearing no.DL-5SCB-3768. When he reached at Defence Colony, New Delhi, a vehicle/car bearing no. MH-02CD-2336 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) being driven in rash and negligent manner hit claimant from right side. Due to the impact, claimant fell on the road and sustained fracture on his left leg and grievous injuries. The claimant was removed to Mool Sariq Ahmad (Dar) vs Ashok Kumar Gandi (4/20, Dc) on 23 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134722225/ 1 Chand hospital from where he was shifted to Lok Nayak Hospital. 3. Pursuant to the directions of concerned criminal court, an FIR no. 0004/2020 u/s 279/338 IPC was registered on 10.01.2020 against the driver of the offending vehicle. After investigation, chargesheet was filed before concerned criminal court against the driver of the offending vehicle while present DAR was filed before this Tribunal. 4. Respondent no.1 is driver-cum-owner of the offending vehicle. Respondent no.2 is the insurance company with which the offending vehicle was insured. Despite opportunity, Respondent no.1 did not file any reply. Respondent no.2/insurance company filed its reply denying the negligence of Respondent no.1 and claiming accident to have occurred due to sole negligence of the petitioner. MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 2 Of 21 BK It is however not denied that the offending vehicle was insured with Respondent no.2 at the time of accident. 5. Vide order dated 06.09.2021, following issues were framed. 1. Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 30.09.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of driver of vehicle no. MH-02CD-2336 being driven & owned by R1 and insured with R2(inadvertently mentioned as R3)? OPP 2. Whether the injured is entitled to compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP. 3. Relief. 6. Evidence was recorded through learned Local Commissioner. To prove his claim, petitioner Sariq Ahmad led his evidence by examining himself as PW-1 by way of affidavit as Ex.PW1/A. He reiterated the facts as of the DAR. On 30.09.2019, after the accident, he was given First Aid in Mool Chand hospital and thereafter shifted to Lok Nayak hospital. On 21.11.2019, he again admitted in Lok Nayak hospital and he underwent a surgery. He was discharged on 28.11.2019 and thereafter he was out patient. He deposed that he spent Rs.1,00,000/- on his treatment, Rs.25,000/- on conveyance, Rs.30,000/- on special diet and Rs.50,000/- on attendant. He was doing the work of supplying bakery items from shop to shop and earning Rs.20,000/- p.m. He relied upon documents i.e. discharge slip as Ex.PW-1/1, OPD card/medical record as Ex.PW-1/2, Medical bills as Ex.PW-1/3. ID proof as Ex.PW-1/4 and DAR as Ex.PW-1/5, Education certificate as Ex.PW-1/6. He was cross- examined by Ld. counsel for insurance company and Respondent MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 3 Of 21 BK no.1. No evidence has been led on behalf of the respondents. 7. Final arguments in details were addressed on behalf of the claimant/injured and the insurance company. On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, Sariq Ahmad (Dar) vs Ashok Kumar Gandi (4/20, Dc) on 23 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134722225/ 2 issue wise findings are as under: Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 30.09.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of driver of vehicle no. MH-02CD-2336 being driven & owned by R1 and insured with R2(inadvertently mentioned as R3)? OPP 8. Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. 9. In the instant case, petitioner/injured Sariq Ahmad examined himself to prove the factum as well as manner of accident. Despite cross-examination, respondent no.1 did not put any suggestion disputing the occurrence of the accident. As regards rash and negligent driving by Respondent no.1 , it is seen MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 4 Of 21 BK from the site plan that the accident occurred in the center of a crossing. Certainly, at such spot, driver of the offending vehicle ought to have been more careful and should have driven his vehicle at a slow speed. Had he maintained a slow speed, the accident could have been averted or at least the impact would have been much less than what the petitioner suffered.
texts.arguments: (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken. 10. In National Insurance Co. vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. To rebut the claim of the petitioner he has not led any evidence in his defence. It may further be noted that in Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310, it was held that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him. Thus, it stands proved that the petitioner suffered injuries in road traffic accident due to rash and negligence of Respondent no.1. Contributory negligence 12. Learned counsel for insurance company has raised a defence qua contributory negligence on the part of the injured, pleading that injured was driving his vehicle/motorcycle without a driving licence. During cross-examination, petitioner/PW-1 could not produce his driving licence and stated that he lost his driving licence at the time of accident. He admitted that he never got lodged any complaint qua losing his driving licence. In fact, it is relevant to note that the petitioner admitted during the cross- Sariq Ahmad (Dar) vs Ashok Kumar Gandi (4/20, Dc) on 23 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134722225/ 3 MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 5 Of 21 BK examination that even on the date of his cross-examination, he had come to the court on his motorbike without a driving licence. Further, the site plan shows that the accident occurred in a middle of busy crossing and the accident could have been averted had petitioner been more careful and cautious about the vehicles coming from other sides. The fact that the petitioner did not hold a driving licence at the time of the accident in 2019 and continuous to drive a motorcycle even in 2023 when his cross- examination was conducted, goes to show that the petitioner lacks basic driving skills to drive a motorcycle. There is also no evidence that petitioner was wearing a helmet. Further, it has come in evidence that the petitioner was carrying two boxes of deliverables on his motorbike. While the petitioner claims that both the boxes were empty after delivery at the time of accident, it is the defence that both the boxes contained heavy goods that caused the motorcycle to disbalance. During cross-examination , petitioner admitted that he was carrying six bags and one box containing snacks but he could not tell the weight(even by way of approximation) of any of the box or bag before or after delivering the same. This raises and adverse inference against the petitioner. Thus, it is possible that the unproportionate weight of the bags and boxes on the motorcycle of the petitioner would have caused his vehicle to disbalance. This also creates doubt if the petitioner was skilled to drive a motorcycle for commercial use. Considering the above position. petitioner is held to have contributed at least 50% to the accident. A deduction of 50% is thus liable to be made from the total compensation amount. 15. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680. The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 7 Of 21 BK his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. 16. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following: Pecuniary damages (Special damages) (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising: (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment; (b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. (iii) Future medical expenses. (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 16.6. Observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajkumar v. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 17 Of 21 BK indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance Sariq Ahmad (Dar) vs Ashok Kumar Gandi (4/20, Dc) on 23 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134722225/ 11 of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation, investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of MACT NO.255/20 Sariq Ahmad v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi P.No. 18 Of 21 BK the guidelines issued by this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants.
